newsitem.title: USA: Seattle's mayor will not seek third term.
newsitem.headline: Seattle's mayor will not seek third term.

text.p: Seattle Mayor Norm Rice said Thursday he will not seek a third four-year term, declaring the time had come to "pass the torch" after 19 years in city government.

"It felt like a good time to pass the torch on to someone else," Rice, Seattle's first black mayor, told a news conference. "I think I've laid down a legacy and a course of action that can sustain itself with or without me."
Rice, 53, has served as mayor of the city of 535,000 since 1989, when he was elected after 11 years on City Council.

One expert on politics in the overwhelmingly Democratic city said Rice's announcement would open the field to a "cast of thousands" of potential candidates. One council member has already announced plans to run in the non-partisan September primary.

Rice's political career stalled when he lost last year's primary for governor and then failed to be appointed secretary of housing and urban development by President Clinton, as many had expected. But he said those disappointments had nothing to do with his decision and he would not rule out possible future bids for office.

"I feel like I still have a lot to offer this city, this state, this country and I'm going to make sure that I'm still aggressively pursuing those things," he said, adding that he had no specific plans for when his term expires at the end of the year.
His tenure has seen Seattle propelled into the limelight as one of the nation's most livable cities, with its strong economy, mild climate, low crime rate and spectacular setting.
The years of publicity have sparked a backlash "lesser Seattle" movement aimed at limiting the city's growth, but Rice has welcomed new business and tried to manage growth through long-term planning.

In a letter to City Council President Jan Drago announcing his decision, Rice said crime in Seattle had fallen to its lowest level in 16 years and he said he had helped put the city on solid financial ground by cutting government growth.
He predicted a $500 million downtown revitalisation programme would spark a "real economic boom" for the city over the next few years.
The popular "Mayor Nice" was elected to a second term in 1993 with 67 percent of the vote and likely would have won a third term easily, political analysts said.
